explanation: Sweet potatoes are native to tropical America, yet Polynesians grew them centuries before 1492. Many researchers think Polynesian voyagers brought them back; others argue seeds drifted across on their own.

claims.text: Polynesians were growing sweet potatoes by about AD 1300 at the latest; remains from Mangaia in the Cook Islands have been dated to about AD 1000.
Christopher Columbus reached the Americas in 1492.
Sweet potatoes are native to tropical America.
Researchers debate whether Polynesian voyagers brought sweet potatoes from South America or the plants spread across the Pacific naturally.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: One source gives a radiocarbon range of 1210–1400 CE for Cook Islands sweet potato. A 2010 PNAS paper treats that same Mangaia date as the earliest presence of sweet potato in Mangaia. Other sources put it earlier. One says the find is carbon dated between 988 and 1155 AD, and a 2010s Antiquity-based review cites AD 1000–1100 radiocarbon chronology on unidentified charcoal from Tangatatau rockshelter on Mangaia. A PNAS chicken study describes the date as indirect, ≈AD 1000. ... The most cautious summary is that Mangaia's sweet potato dates to roughly the 11th to 15th centuries CE depending on the sample and calibration, which predates European contact.

claimResults.note: Checker doubt. Tier A and B sources disagree on the date of the Mangaia remains (988 to 1155, or 1210 to 1400 CE), so neither 'about AD 1000' nor 'by about AD 1300 at the latest' is agreed. Every date given is before 1492, so the key holds. An earlier call (counted in p.food.0167's record) misread the question as contested; it is not used.
